job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a small company in Brno that makes control boards for packaging machines. I studied electrical and computer engineering, and my final project was a sensor that counts bottles on a line. Most days I write firmware in C, test boards on my bench and chat with an AI model about every second bug. After work I run a little side business selling custom sensor kits to hobbyists online. I rent a room with my friend Tomas, and on Sundays I go to Mass with my grandmother and have lunch at her house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools I use every day already do enough for me. I'd tell friends not to believe the doom. At work I'd keep getting more done with the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be glad. If AI plateaus I keep my advantage because I know how to use it, and most people don't. The one worry I'd have is the euro and rising costs, because wages don't go up as fast as rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on and grow the side business. I'd put some of my pay into the kit shop, maybe hire a part-timer to pack orders. I'd also save for a flat in Brno with Tereza, my girlfriend, in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit pleased. I like it when the future looks the same as today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said wages don't keep up with rent. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My room costs 9,000 crowns and my salary is good for Brno, but a flat for two is about four million. Tereza and I have 600,000 saved. My grandma says her generation bought with less, and that's true, but wages then went up faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the kit shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 40 orders a month, and it makes maybe 12,000 crowns profit after parts. It started as a hobby with a few forum posts, and one customer from Germany ordered 20 units. My boss knows and doesn't mind, as long as I don't use company time.

say: The tools I use every day already do enough for me.
I'd tell friends not to believe the **doom**.
think: If AI plateaus I keep an **advantage**, because I know how to use it and most people don't.
Wages don't rise as fast as **rent**.
do: Grow the **kit shop**, maybe with a part-timer to pack orders.
Save for a **flat** in Brno with my girlfriend.
feel: I feel **calm and pleased** when the future looks like today.
S0.quote: My grandma says her generation bought with less, and that's true, but wages then went up faster.
fieldNote: He is secure and uses AI as an **advantage** over colleagues.
His shop shows a real appetite for risk and ownership.
Housing is his only steady worry.

steps.text: Hire a part-timer to pack kit orders in the evenings
Save towards a flat in Brno with my girlfriend
Keep using the AI model for firmware bugs every day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big opportunity if you're quick. I'd tell friends to start businesses, not wait for jobs. At work I'd say we should use AI to design the next board, and I'd offer to lead it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think some firms get squeezed, especially those that only write code. But hardware is physical, and boards still need people who can solder and test. I'd be better off than a pure software guy, and I'd like to prove it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to lead an AI-assisted design project at work. I'd expand the kit shop to sell a small AI sensor module. And I'd put some money in a few shares in European robotics and chip firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous, because speed also means mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said speed means mistakes. When would that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I ship a board that an AI designed and I trust it too much. I once let it pick a resistor value for a heater circuit and it was off by a factor of ten. The test caught it, but a customer wouldn't. So I check each part against the datasheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an AI sensor module be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small board with a chip that can recognise a few sounds or vibrations. Farmers or small factories could stick it on a machine and get a text when something sounds wrong. It's a small thing, but a lot of small firms would pay 50 euros for it.

say: It's a big opportunity if you're **quick**, and people should start businesses, not wait for jobs.
At work I'd offer to lead an AI-assisted board design.
think: Firms that only write code get squeezed, but **hardware** still needs people who can solder and test.
I'd be better off than a pure software person.
do: Lead an **AI-assisted design** project at work.
Add a small **AI sensor module** to the kit shop and buy some chip-firm shares.
feel: I feel **excited**, a bit nervous because speed means mistakes.
S1.quote: I once let it pick a resistor value for a heater circuit and it was off by a factor of ten.
fieldNote: He is **eager** and sees the change as a market.
His checks against datasheets show a careful side.
Hardware work gives him a head start over software peers.

steps.text: Offer to lead an AI-assisted design for our next control board
Build a small AI vibration sensor module to sell for 50 euros
Buy shares in European chip and robotics firms with 200 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's too fast and nobody will be ready, but it's also a land rush. I'd tell friends to work and not wait for the state to save them. At work I'd say we need to move before our competitors do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a lot of engineering jobs vanish in two years, maybe mine. I'd rather own something than be an employee in that world. If thinking work is cheap, whoever has customers and sells real things wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time on the kit shop and a new line of products, and I'd talk to my boss about a part-time contract. I'd use my savings for stock, but not all of it. I'd also look for a partner with a workshop, because robots for hands-on work come three years later and I'd want to be in that business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of fear and hunger. I'd sleep badly and work a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather own something. Why does ownership matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a salary is a favour from a boss, and ownership is something I earned. My grandfather lost his job in 1993 when the factory closed, and then he opened a bakery. That shop fed the family for 25 years. Nobody gave it to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about people who can't start something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard, and I'd help where I can, with advice and maybe jobs at my shop. But I don't believe in waiting for a handout. Family, church and neighbours come first, and then the government.

say: It's too fast and nobody will be ready, but it's also a **land rush**.
At work I'd say we must move before competitors do.
think: A lot of engineering jobs vanish in two years, **maybe mine**.
In that world, whoever has customers and sells real things wins.
do: Go full-time on the **kit shop** and ask my boss about a part-time contract.
Find a partner with a **workshop**, to be ready for robots in hands-on work.
feel: I feel **fear and hunger**, sleeping badly and working a lot.
S2.quote: A salary is a favour from a boss, and ownership is something I earned.
fieldNote: He answers danger by **owning something**, shaped by his grandfather's bakery.
He has savings and customers, so he stays uneasy not anxious.
His help for others goes through family and church first.

steps.text: Ask my boss for a part-time contract and run the shop full-time
Spend half my savings on parts and stock for the shop
Find a partner with a workshop to build robot parts later

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if people are decisive. I'd tell friends to take risks and work. At work I'd propose to build our own AI-based test equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm optimistic. By 2031 my company probably needs fewer engineers, but I'd be on my own by then, with a shop and a team. The robots arriving in 2034 are a market for sensors and controllers, which is what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shop into a proper company in two years, hire two engineers and maybe move into a small unit. I'd marry Tereza and buy a flat in Brno. I'd keep using every new AI tool as it appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic. I feel like the road is open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build for the robots coming in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The small unglamorous bits: touch sensors for grippers, cheap boards that tell a robot arm where its limit is. Big companies make the arms, but somebody has to supply the senses. I'd like to be that supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Tereza. What does she think of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a nurse, so she's calm about it. She says people always need care and she'll always have work. She worries I'll work too much, and she's probably right. We agreed on a rule, no work on Sundays.

say: Five years is enough if people are **decisive**, so take risks and work.
I'd propose we build our own AI-based test equipment at work.
think: By 2031 my company probably needs fewer engineers, but I'd be on my own with a **shop** and a team.
Robots arriving in 2034 are a market for **sensors** and controllers.
do: Grow the shop into a proper **company** in two years and hire two engineers.
Marry my girlfriend and buy a **flat** in Brno.
feel: I feel **optimistic**, as if the road is open.
S3.quote: Big companies make the arms, but somebody has to supply the senses.
fieldNote: He sees robots in 2034 as a **customer base**.
His girlfriend's nursing job is a stable counterweight.
The no-work-on-Sundays rule shows his faith and family limits.

steps.text: Turn the kit shop into a registered company within two years
Hire two engineers to build touch sensors for robot grippers
Marry my girlfriend and buy a flat in Brno

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and it'll be a good time to build. I'd tell friends to learn by doing and to avoid debt. At work I'd say keep an eye on what customers pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm happy. By 32 I'd be running a business, married, maybe with kids. I'd worry that people who sit back lose out, and I'd feel for them, but I don't think the state should carry everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the company, give jobs to a few young people, and put money into a small family fund. I'd give to the parish and pay for my grandmother's care. I'd learn whatever tools show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ambitious. I feel I can shape it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't think the state should carry everyone. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a safety net is fine for the sick and the very old, but young people should work and learn. My generation will be tempted to wait for a cheque. I'd rather see apprenticeships and small business loans than a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your grandmother's care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay for a nurse a few days a week, and I'd visit on Sundays after Mass. She raised me while my parents worked abroad for a few years. I'd want her to stay in her own flat as long as she can.

say: Ten years is plenty, and it'll be a good time to **build**.
I'd tell friends to learn by doing and avoid debt.
think: By 32 I'd run a **business**, be married and maybe have kids.
The state shouldn't carry everyone, though I feel for people who sit back.
do: Build the company and give jobs to a few **young people**.
Pay for my grandmother's **care** and give to the parish.
feel: I feel **calm and ambitious**, as if I can shape it.
S4.quote: I'd rather see apprenticeships and small business loans than a basic income.
fieldNote: His traditional outlook shows in his **self-reliance** and respect for church and family.
Ten years lets him be generous as well as ambitious.
His care for his grandmother is concrete and funded.

steps.text: Hire two young apprentices at the company in year four
Pay for a nurse to visit my grandmother three days a week
Keep avoiding debt and add to a family savings fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, though I'd manage. Two years is too fast for the people who don't have savings or a skill. What would help is cheap business loans, apprenticeships and not too many rules getting in the way of people trying things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people expect traditional folks to be against new tech. I use AI every day and I go to church. I don't see a conflict.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day and I go to church. I don't see a conflict.
portrait: Ben is a **22-year-old** firmware engineer in Brno who also runs a small online sensor-kit shop.
He is traditional and free-market, goes to Mass and uses AI **every day**.
His grandfather's bakery taught him that **ownership** beats a salary.
He stays calm in most worlds and is only **uneasy** in a two-year jump.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, for people without savings or a skill.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap business loans**, apprenticeships and fewer rules in the way.
